column1: # source: per-suite timings from the green Linux main CI runs 39180908042 (head
#   SUITE_CHANGED_SINCE); each row is the mean of the runs that suite appeared in.
#   990 unique suites; no row is local-measured. Timings are a snapshot, not a
#   worst-case bound. Replay on run 39180908042: max/min 2.454 before, 1.304 after;
#   slowest shard 2800s before, 2304s after (suite time only, excluding setup/waits).
#   ran ~2300s. It is now four case-range parts (-a..-d); their rows split the
#   2301s mean in proportion to each part's case count (249/239/269/261 of 1018).
#   With that suite no longer the floor, the 22w balance check sees the stale
#   test-stop-worker.sh row (117s here, 317s measured); it is refreshed to 317.
# The quarantined suites (SKIP_LIST, HIMMEL-3196) have no row.
# Read by scripts/ci/run-shell-tests.sh to assign --shard <i>/<n> by a greedy
# longest-first bin-pack instead of round-robin ($SUITE_DURATIONS overrides this
# path). Keys are the suite path exactly as that runner PRINTS it, which is also
# exactly what the regeneration command below harvests out of a job log — so the
# spelling written here and the spelling matched against cannot drift apart.
# STALENESS: this is a snapshot, bumped on demand, not a CI-maintained file. It
# tunes balance only; it can never change which suites run. A suite absent from
# it is assigned the median of the rows present and runs like any other — never
# dropped. A row naming a suite that no longer exists is ignored for assignment,
# though its duration still counts toward that median. If the file is missing or
# unreadable the runner says so once on stderr and falls back to round-robin; if
# it is present but no row parses the runner says THAT once and packs anyway,
# which with every duration equal is round-robin by another route. So a stale or
# broken ledger costs wall clock, nothing else; refresh it when the corpus has
# moved enough that the shard times skew.
